passages.t: A census, and a birth in Bethlehem
passages.happening:
The Roman emperor, Caesar Augustus, orders a census, a count of the people. Everyone goes to his own town to be registered. So Joseph goes from Nazareth in Galilee down to Bethlehem in Judea, “the city of David” (verse 4), because he belongs to David's family. Mary goes with him. She is pledged to marry him, and she is expecting a child.

While they are in Bethlehem, the baby comes. Mary gives birth to her firstborn son. “She wrapped Him in swaddling cloths and laid Him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Augustus was the most powerful man in the world. He ruled from Rome from 27 BC until AD 14, and cities across the empire honoured him as a bringer of peace. Luke begins with the emperor's order and ends with a baby in a feeding trough. The emperor thinks he is counting his people. Luke shows God using the emperor's order to bring David's son to David's town.

Swaddling cloths were strips of cloth wrapped snugly round a newborn baby. It was what any careful mother did. A manger is a feeding trough for animals.

‘No room in the inn.’ The Greek word Luke uses here, kataluma, is the word he later uses for the ‘guest room’ where Jesus eats the last supper (22:11). When Luke means a paid inn, in the story of the Good Samaritan, he uses a different word (10:34). So many scholars now think Mary and Joseph were staying in a family house, and that its guest room was full or too small. Some scholars point out that in the village houses of the region, animals were kept in a lower part of the main room, so a manger could stand in the family's own living space. Others think the word simply means ‘a place to stay’. Either way, notice who is missing. There is no innkeeper in Luke's story, and no one turns them away. The cruel innkeeper of Christmas plays is not in the text.

The difficulty of the census. Luke says this was “the first census to take place while Quirinius was governor of Syria” (verse 2). Quirinius became governor of Syria in AD 6, about ten years after King Herod died, and Luke and Matthew both place the birth while Herod was alive. No writer outside Luke tells of a Roman census in Herod's kingdom. This is a real difficulty, and scholars have given several explanations: that Luke joined the famous census of AD 6 to the time of the birth by mistake; that Quirinius held an earlier command in Syria; that the Greek word for ‘first’ here means ‘before’; that an earlier count was begun under Herod and finished later. The book page sets these out. These notes do not settle it.
passages.ot: Bethlehem had a long story. It was David's home town; young David was out ‘tending the sheep’ near there when the prophet Samuel came to anoint him (1 Samuel 16:11). And the prophet Micah had promised, “But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel” (Micah 5:2). Luke does not quote Micah, as Matthew does (Matthew 2:6). He simply lets Jewish hearers notice where the child is born.
passages.hard:
Did the census really happen as Luke says? Faithful scholars disagree, and the honest answer is that the evidence does not settle it. What can be said is this. The question is about a date and an official, not about whether Jesus was a real man born in a real place. Luke elsewhere names Roman rulers with care, which is why some give him the benefit of the doubt here, and others reply that care elsewhere does not prove him right here. A reader can hold the question open and still read the story.

Why ‘firstborn’? The word does not settle whether Mary had children later; Christians disagree about that (see the notes on Matthew 1). In Jewish law the firstborn son belonged to God in a special way (Exodus 13:2), and that is the point Luke will make in verses 22 and 23.
passages.asks: God's Son arrived in a borrowed room, laid in a feeding trough, in a town crowded by a foreign emperor's order. Nothing about the scene looked important. Where do you look for God? Luke suggests that he is often found in the places we would pass by.

passages.happening:
In the fields nearby, shepherds are keeping watch over their flocks at night. Suddenly an angel of the Lord stands before them, the glory of the Lord shines all around, and they are terrified.

The angel says, “Do not be afraid! For behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people: Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord!” (verses 10-11). The sign will be a baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger.

Then a great crowd of heavenly beings appears, praising God: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men on whom His favor rests!” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Shepherds lived outdoors with their flocks, often through the night, guarding them from thieves and wild animals. They were working men, not people of rank. Many sermons say that shepherds were despised outcasts. The evidence for that comes mostly from Jewish writings set down well after Jesus' day; one saying in the Mishnah, written down around AD 200, lists herding among trades a father should not teach his son because they tempt a man to steal (Mishnah Kiddushin 4:14). How far that reflects the first century is debated, and the Bible itself honours shepherds. What can be said is that the news came first to ordinary working men in a field at night, not to priests in the temple or to the emperor in Rome.

The angel's words would have startled anyone who knew how the empire spoke. About 9 BC, the cities of the Roman province of Asia, in what is now Turkey, decreed that Augustus's birthday was the beginning of ‘good news’ for the world and called him a savior. Now an angel announces good news, a Savior and peace, and gives them to a baby in a manger.

‘Christ’ is the Greek for ‘Messiah’, the anointed king Israel was waiting for. ‘Lord’ was the word the Greek Bible used for God himself. The angel puts the titles side by side.
passages.ot:
For Jewish hearers, shepherds called up the best of their story. David was a shepherd before he was a king. And the LORD himself was Israel's shepherd: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1). Through Ezekiel, God promised to shepherd his flock himself and to set over them “one shepherd, My servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23). It is fitting that the shepherd-king's heir is announced first to shepherds near David's town.

‘Peace on earth’ recalls the promise of a child whose rule brings peace with no end (Isaiah 9:6-7).
passages.hard: What does ‘on earth peace to men on whom His favor rests’ mean? Older English Bibles, like the King James Version, say ‘good will toward men’. The difference in Greek is a single letter. The oldest copies of Luke have the reading behind ‘on whom His favor rests’, and most modern Bibles follow them. It does not mean God's peace is only for a favoured few who earned it. It means the peace comes from God's favour, his free kindness, not from human goodwill. The angels are praising what God gives.
passages.asks: The first people to hear the news of Jesus were working men on the night shift. God did not wait for the important people. If you feel ordinary, unnoticed or far from religious life, this is your story too. The angel's first words are still for you: “Do not be afraid!”

passages.t: They went and saw, and told
passages.happening:
When the angels leave, the shepherds say to one another, “Let us go to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us” (verse 15). They hurry off and find Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in the manger, just as they were told.

They tell everyone what the angel said about the child, and all who hear are amazed. “But Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart” (verse 19). The shepherds go back to their flocks, glorifying and praising God for everything they had heard and seen.
passages.hearers:
The shepherds do three things, and Luke's readers would see in them the pattern of faith. They go to see for themselves. They tell others what they saw. And they go back to their ordinary work, praising God. Nothing about their jobs has changed. Everything about how they do them has.

Mary does something different. She keeps quiet and thinks. The word ‘pondered’ means turning something over, putting the pieces side by side to see how they fit. Luke says it twice in this chapter (verses 19 and 51). Many readers have taken that as a quiet hint about where some of Luke's stories came from. Luke said in his first sentence that he learned from eyewitnesses (1:2), and no one saw these things more closely than Mary. That is a guess, but a reasonable one.
passages.ot: The shepherds' eagerness to ‘go and see’ answers an old sorrow in Scripture. Isaiah complained that “the ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger, but Israel does not know” (Isaiah 1:3). Now humble people come to a manger and know who lies in it. The shepherds also echo the Psalms, which call on all who have seen God's works to tell of them and praise him.
passages.hard: Did everyone who heard the shepherds believe? In the story, ‘all who heard it were amazed’ (verse 18). Luke does not say that everyone believed. Amazement is not yet faith. Many who heard would have forgotten in a week. Luke keeps that honesty all through his book: wonder is a beginning, not an end.
passages.asks: The shepherds told what they had seen and went back to work praising God. Mary kept quiet and pondered. Both are ways of receiving good news. Which do you need more today: to tell someone what God has done, or to sit still and let it sink in?

passages.t: Named, and presented in the temple
passages.happening:
On the eighth day the baby is circumcised and given the name Jesus, the name the angel gave before he was conceived.

When the days for Mary's purification under the law of Moses are complete, Joseph and Mary take Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord. They do it as the law says: “Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord” (verse 23). And they offer the sacrifice the law sets out: “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Three old customs from the law of Moses come together here.

Circumcision on the eighth day marked a Jewish boy as part of God's covenant people (Leviticus 12:3).

Purification. After giving birth to a son, a mother waited forty days, seven and then thirty-three, before going to the sanctuary again (Leviticus 12:2-4). Then she brought an offering. This was not a judgment on her or on childbirth. In the law, contact with birth and death, the great edges of life, set a person apart for a time.

The offering tells us something. The law asked for a lamb and a bird. But if a family could not afford a lamb, two doves or two pigeons would do (Leviticus 12:8). Mary and Joseph bring the poor family's offering. Jesus grew up in a household with little money.

The firstborn. Every firstborn son belonged to God in a special way, because God had spared Israel's firstborn when he brought them out of Egypt (Exodus 13:2). So Jesus is brought and presented.
passages.ot:
Luke mentions ‘the Law’ five times in this chapter (verses 22, 23, 24, 27 and 39). He wants his readers to see a faithful Jewish family keeping every command. Jesus was born into Israel's covenant, not outside it.

The scene also recalls Hannah, who brought her young son Samuel to the house of the LORD and gave him to God (1 Samuel 1:24-28). And it begins to fulfil Malachi 3:1, “Then the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple.” Malachi's hearers might have pictured a grand arrival. The Lord comes to his temple as a baby in the arms of a poor couple.
passages.hard: Why did Jesus need to be purified, circumcised or presented, if he was the Son of God? Christians answer that he did not come to stand apart from his people but to share their life completely. Paul later wrote that God sent his Son, “born of a woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4:4). He kept the law from his first week of life. The church has seen in this how fully he became one of us.
passages.asks: Mary and Joseph could only afford the smallest offering, and it was accepted. God has never measured gifts by their size. What small, ordinary act of faithfulness can you offer this week, and trust that it is enough?

passages.t: Simeon: ‘My eyes have seen Your salvation’
passages.happening:
In Jerusalem lives a man named Simeon, “righteous and devout” (verse 25). He is waiting for “the consolation of Israel”. The Holy Spirit has told him he will not die before he has seen the Lord's Christ.

Led by the Spirit, he goes into the temple courts just as Mary and Joseph bring Jesus in. He takes the baby in his arms and praises God: “Sovereign Lord, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace. For my eyes have seen Your salvation, which You have prepared in the sight of all people, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel” (verses 29-32).

Mary and Joseph are amazed. Then Simeon blesses them and speaks to Mary. This child will cause the falling and rising of many in Israel. He will be a sign that people speak against, and the secret thoughts of many will come out. And then to Mary herself: “a sword will pierce your soul as well” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Simeon's song is called the Nunc Dimittis, from its first words in Latin, ‘now you dismiss’. Christians have sung it at the end of the day for many centuries, at night prayer, as a prayer for a peaceful sleep and a peaceful death.

‘Dismiss’ is the word for a master releasing a servant from his watch. Simeon is like a guard who has stood at his post all night, waiting for the morning. Now it has come. He can go.

‘The consolation of Israel’ meant the comfort God had promised his people after all their suffering. Simeon had waited his whole life for it. He finds it in a baby.

He says something that would surprise many Jewish hearers: this child is a light for the Gentiles, the nations outside Israel, as well as glory for Israel. From his first weeks, Jesus is for the whole world.
passages.ot:
‘The consolation of Israel’ comes from Isaiah: “Comfort, comfort My people,” says your God (Isaiah 40:1). Simeon's song draws on Isaiah's servant, whom God would make “a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6), and on the promise that “all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God” (Isaiah 52:10).

His warning that the child will make many fall and rise recalls Isaiah 8:14, where the LORD himself is “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” to Israel. Later Jesus calls himself the stone that the builders rejected (20:17).
passages.hard:
What is the sword that will pierce Mary's soul? Most readers take it as the grief Mary would feel when her son was rejected and killed. She would stand near the cross (John 19:25). Simeon tells her, at the happiest moment of her life, that love for this child will cost her deeply.

If you have lost a child, or watched a child suffer, these words may reach a sore place. Simeon does not explain away Mary's coming pain, and Scripture does not ask you to explain away yours. You are allowed to grieve, and to refuse comfort for a time. Please do not carry it alone. Speak to someone you trust, a pastor or a grief counsellor, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service.

The words ‘sign that will be spoken against’ also say something hard. Jesus will divide people. Some will rise by trusting him; some will fall by refusing him. He will bring hidden thoughts into the light.
passages.asks: Simeon waited a lifetime, and was ready to die in peace once he had held the child. What are you waiting for? Simeon's peace did not come from getting everything he wanted. It came from seeing God keep his word. Could that be enough for you?

passages.happening:
A prophetess named Anna is also there. She is the daughter of Phanuel, from the tribe of Asher. She was married for seven years, and then lived as a widow into great old age. She never leaves the temple. She worships night and day, fasting and praying.

Coming up at that very moment, she gives thanks to God and speaks about the child to everyone who is waiting for “the redemption of Jerusalem” (verse 38).

When Mary and Joseph have done everything the law requires, they go home to Nazareth. “And the Child grew and became strong. He was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon Him” (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
Luke often pairs a man and a woman: Zechariah and Mary, Simeon and Anna, later a shepherd with his sheep and a woman with her coin. Here two old people, one man and one woman, both full of the Spirit, both waiting, recognize the child when no one else does.

Anna is called a prophetess, a woman who speaks God's word. Few women in Scripture are given that title. Luke even names her father and her tribe, Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. He wants her remembered.

Widows were often poor and easily overlooked. Anna had lived most of her life alone. The Greek of verse 37 can be read two ways: that she was a widow until she was eighty-four, or that she had been a widow for eighty-four years. Either way, she had spent decades in prayer.

‘The redemption of Jerusalem’ meant God buying back, setting free, his city and his people. Anna tells everyone who shares that hope that it has arrived.
passages.ot:
Anna's long years of prayer and fasting recall the faithful women of Israel's story. She is a prophetess like Miriam (Exodus 15:20), Deborah (Judges 4:4) and Huldah (2 Kings 22:14). And her hope for the redemption of Jerusalem echoes Isaiah, “for the LORD has comforted His people; He has redeemed Jerusalem” (Isaiah 52:9).

The summary of Jesus' growth (verse 40) echoes what Scripture says of the boy Samuel, who “continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man” (1 Samuel 2:26).
passages.hard: Is Anna's life of fasting and prayer meant for everyone? Not in the same form. Most people cannot live in a temple, and Scripture honours ordinary work and family life. But Anna shows that a life many would call empty, old, widowed and alone, can be full before God. Luke gives her the last word in the temple scene.
passages.asks: Anna's years of waiting were not wasted. They made her ready to see. If you are older, alone, or feel your best years are past, Anna's story says that God has not finished with you. And if you are young, who are the Annas around you, whose prayers you have never noticed?

passages.t: The boy in His Father's house
passages.happening:
Every year Jesus' parents go to Jerusalem for the feast of Passover. When he is twelve, they go as usual. On the way home, they travel a whole day before they realize he is not with their group of relatives and friends.

They go back and search for three days. At last they find him in the temple courts, “sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions” (verse 46). Everyone is amazed at how much he understands.

His mother says, “Child, why have You done this to us?” and, “Your father and I have been anxiously searching for You” (verse 48). He answers, “Why were you looking for Me?” and, “Did you not know that I had to be in My Father's house?” (verse 49). They do not understand.

He goes home with them to Nazareth and obeys them. His mother keeps all these things in her heart. “And Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man” (verse 52).
passages.hearers:
The law asked Jewish men to go up to Jerusalem for three great feasts each year (Deuteronomy 16:16). Mary goes too, and the family goes every year. Luke is showing a devout household.

Pilgrims from Galilee travelled together in large groups of family and neighbours, often on foot over several days. In such a crowd, parents could easily assume a twelve-year-old was with cousins or friends. Losing him was not careless; finding him missing was terrifying.

Twelve was close to the age when, by later Jewish teaching, a boy became responsible for keeping the commandments himself; a Jewish saying added to the Mishnah sets it at thirteen. Jesus is on the edge of growing up.

Notice what he is doing in the temple. He is not lecturing the teachers. He is sitting with them, listening and asking questions, as a good student would. They are amazed at his understanding.

These are Jesus' first words in Luke's Gospel. And the first thing he says is about God as ‘My Father’.
passages.ot:
The verse that closes the chapter echoes the boy Samuel again, who grew “in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man” (1 Samuel 2:26). Samuel too grew up in God's house, at the shrine at Shiloh. Luke's readers would see the line running from Hannah's son to Mary's.

The temple was where Israel met God, the house God had promised to fill with his presence. Jesus calls it his Father's house. In Malachi the Lord comes suddenly to his temple (Malachi 3:1). Here he comes as a boy, quietly, and calls it home.
passages.hard:
Was Jesus disobedient to his parents? He stayed behind without telling them, and they suffered for it. But Luke goes straight on to say that he went home and ‘was obedient to them’ (verse 51). Jesus' answer is not rude; it is surprised. He assumed they would know where to find him. Older translations say ‘about My Father's business’; the Greek can carry both senses, being in his Father's house and about his Father's work.

How could the Son of God grow in wisdom? Luke says plainly that he did (verse 52). The church has confessed that Jesus is fully God and fully human. As a human being he really learned, really grew, really had a childhood. That is part of what it means that God became one of us.

A word for parents. Mary and Joseph lost their son for three days and did not understand his answer. If you have a child who has wandered or whom you cannot understand, you are not the first. Even this family knew fear and confusion. Mary kept the things she did not understand in her heart, and waited.
passages.asks: Jesus knew who his Father was, and still went home and obeyed his parents. Knowing God's call did not make him too important for ordinary duty. Where is God asking you to be faithful in small, daily things, even when you sense there is more to come?
